title: Two messages suffice for quantum interactive proof systems
problem: A quantum interactive proof lets a polynomial-time quantum verifier exchange messages with an all-powerful prover. With polynomially many messages such systems decide exactly \(\mathsf{PSPACE}\), and Kitaev and Watrous showed in 2000 that three messages always suffice. Classically, by contrast, every constant-message proof collapses to two messages, the class \(\mathsf{AM}\), which is believed to be far weaker than \(\mathsf{PSPACE}\). Whether quantum proofs can be compressed further, to a single question and a single answer, had been open since Watrous's 2003 paper.
result: Every quantum interactive proof can be compressed to two messages: \(\mathsf{QIP}(2)=\mathsf{QIP}=\mathsf{PSPACE}\). The verifier's only message consists of halves of EPR pairs (quantum public coins), and after the prover's reply it needs only classical reversible gates, \(\ket0\) and \(\ket+\) ancillas and one Hadamard-basis measurement, with perfect completeness. The proof shows that a sampling problem, Close Image to Uniform, is \(\mathsf{PSPACE}\)-hard with an inverse-polynomial gap, by turning the sum-check protocol for quantified Boolean formulas into a single sampler.
significance: Two messages are the minimum for an interactive proof, so the result settles the round complexity of quantum interactive proofs. It also separates the quantum and classical pictures sharply: a two-message classical proof is believed unable to verify \(\mathsf{PSPACE}\), while two quantum messages verify all of it. For stoquastic verifiers it gives a dichotomy, since one-message stoquastic proofs are contained in \(\mathsf{AM}\) and are believed to equal \(\mathsf{MA}\).
limitations: The verifier's message must be quantum. If it were replaced by classical random bits, the class would be \(\mathsf{QAM}\subseteq\mathsf{BP}\cdot\mathsf{PP}\), and equality with \(\mathsf{PSPACE}\) would collapse the counting hierarchy, so that version is not expected. Before amplification the protocol has completeness 1 and soundness only \(1-\eta^2/2\) with \(\eta=1/(32(T+1)^2)\), where \(T\) grows quadratically with the formula size; a constant gap needs parallel repetition, proved in an appendix that was not read here. The honest prover must apply an isometry that is generally hard to compute. The author states that large language model tools were used interactively at all stages, from exploratory research to writing, and that the manuscript was substantially revised by the author.

description: In a quantum interactive proof the verifier asks, the prover answers, and after polynomially many rounds the verifier accepts or rejects. Completeness says an honest prover convinces the verifier on yes instances; soundness says no prover succeeds with high probability on no instances. Quantum proofs have a striking feature: any such protocol can be parallelized to three messages, and the verifier's single message can even be one random bit. Classically, compressing a polynomial-round proof to a constant number of rounds would collapse the polynomial hierarchy.

The paper removes the last message. In the new protocol the verifier prepares EPR pairs, sends one half of each to the prover, and receives a quantum reply. It then runs a reversible classical circuit and a SWAP test, which is stoquastic: only Toffoli, CNOT and \(X\) gates act before a final Hadamard-basis measurement. Combined with known inclusions, this gives \[\text{qq-}\mathsf{StoqAM}_1=\text{qq-}\mathsf{QAM}=\mathsf{QIP}(2)=\mathsf{QIP}=\mathsf{PSPACE}.\]

The bridge is a promise problem about samplers. A circuit \(\mathcal S\) maps an input \(u\) and a random seed \(r\) to an output \(u'\). In a yes instance some input distribution makes the output exactly uniform; in a no instance every input distribution leaves the output at least \(\eta\) away from uniform in total variation. Hardness comes from the sum-check protocol of Shamir and Shen. The verifier's step from one claim \(P_t(\alpha)=\nu\) to the next becomes one step of a sampler, and the sampler's output can be exactly uniform only when every claim along the chain is consistent, which happens precisely when the quantified Boolean formula is true.

Testing uniformity is natural for a quantum verifier with EPR pairs. The verifier's half of the pairs is maximally mixed whatever the prover does, so the prover must produce inputs and seeds whose image under \(\mathcal S\) reproduces that uniform register coherently. The result also completes a trichotomy for generalized Arthur–Merlin games: any constant-message game in which a later verifier message is quantum equals \(\mathsf{PSPACE}\), while all-classical variants collapse to \(\mathsf{QAM}\) or \(\mathsf{QCAM}\).

methods.technique: Sum-check rounds as a sampler whose image is uniform only for true formulas
methods.explanation: The sum-check verifier checks a chain of claims about polynomials, each derived from the previous one at a random point. Instead of checking a whole transcript, the construction feeds one claim at a time through a sampler and asks whether some input distribution makes the stream of claims look uniformly random.
math:
Claims are triples \((t,\alpha,
u)\) meaning \(P_t(\alpha)=
u\), with \(t\in\{0,\dots,T\}\), \(\alpha\in\mathbb F_q^{m'}\) and \(
u\in\mathbb F_q\). Given a claim and a proposed restriction \(g\), the sampler leaves the claim unchanged unless it is true. A true claim with \(t<T\) is replaced by \((t+1,\alpha[j_t\leftarrow r],g(r))\) for uniform \(r\), and a true claim at \(t=T\) is replaced by \((0,\alpha,P_0(\alpha))\).

Yes case. With honest restrictions, \(g(r)=P_{t+1}(\alpha[j_t\leftarrow r])\) is again a true claim. Start from a uniform triple. Each pair \((t,\alpha)\) carries the true value with probability \(1/q\), and that mass is spread uniformly over the \(q\) points \(\alpha[j_t\leftarrow r]\); each point of round \(t+1\) receives it from exactly \(q\) predecessors. Hence every true claim at \((t',\alpha')\) again has probability \[\frac{1}{(T+1)\,q^{m'}}\cdot\frac1q,\] the uniform value, while false claims keep their uniform mass. The output is exactly uniform. Editorial check: an abstract instance with \(q=5\), \(m'=2\) and \(T=3\) gave a deviation of exactly zero.

No case. Compare the output law with the uniform law on two events: the round is \(T\), which has uniform probability \(1/(T+1)\), and the claim is true, which has uniform probability \(1/q\). The total variation distance bounds both differences, and the paper's weighting \[\mathrm{TV}\ \ge\ \frac{1}{q+1}\Bigl|\tfrac1{T+1}-\Pr[t'=T]\Bigr|+\frac{q}{q+1}\Bigl|\tfrac1q-\Pr[P_{t'}(\alpha')=\nu]\Bigr|\] cancels the unknown \(\Pr[t'=T]\). With \(q=8(T+1)\) this gives \(\mathrm{TV}\ge1/(4q(T+1))=1/(32(T+1)^2)\). Degree reduction keeps \(T+1=O(|\Phi|^2)\), so the gap is inverse-polynomial; an exponentially large field, as in Shamir's original protocol, would make it exponentially small.
methods.transfer: Recasting a multi-round verification as a single Markov step whose stationary law is uniform exactly on consistent inputs converts round-by-round soundness into a distance from uniformity. The same idea can turn other algebraic protocols into sampling problems with polynomial gaps.

methods.technique: Testing a uniform image with EPR halves and a SWAP test
methods.explanation: The verifier keeps one half of each EPR pair, so its register is uniformly random whatever the prover does. A prover who knows a good input distribution can produce a state whose image under the sampler matches that register coherently, and the verifier detects this by uncomputing the sampler and comparing what remains with a fixed product state.
math: Completeness. If \(M_{\mathcal S}p\) is uniform, the honest prover maps each \(\ket{u'}\) on its EPR half to a normalized multiple of \[\sum_{(u,r):\,\mathcal S(u,r)=u'}\sqrt{p(u)}\,\ket u\ket r.\] The normalization is the same for every \(u'\) because each output has probability \(2^{-m_{\rm out}}\). After the verifier applies the inverse of the sampler's reversible circuit, the state is \(\bigl(\sum_u\sqrt{p(u)}\ket u\bigr)\ket+^{\otimes m_+}\ket0^{\otimes m_{\rm out}}\), and a SWAP test against \(\ket+^{\otimes m_+}\ket0^{\otimes m_{\rm out}}\) accepts with certainty.

Soundness. Let \(\ket\psi\) be the joint state before uncomputation; measuring the verifier's register gives the uniform distribution. Any state \(\ket\xi\) produced by running the sampler on \(\ket+^{\otimes m_+}\ket0^{\otimes m_{\rm out}}\) gives outcome law \(M_{\mathcal S}p\) for some \(p\). A measurement cannot increase trace distance, so \[\eta\le\mathrm{TV}(M_{\mathcal S}p,U)\le\sqrt{1-|\langle\psi|\xi\rangle|^2}.\] The SWAP test accepts with probability \((1+\mathrm{Tr}\,\rho_0\rho_1)/2\). Editorial step: since \(\rho_1\) is pure, \(\mathrm{Tr}\,\rho_0\rho_1\) is the largest \(|\langle\psi|\xi\rangle|^2\) over such \(\ket\xi\) by Uhlmann's theorem, so acceptance is at most \(1-\eta^2/2\).

Every gate after the prover's message is reversible classical or the SWAP test, which uses Toffoli and CNOT gates on \(\ket0\) and \(\ket+\) ancillas, and the final measurement is in the Hadamard basis. That is why the verifier is stoquastic, and why the classical-coin version of the same verifier, \(\mathsf{StoqAM}\), only reaches \(\mathsf{AM}\).
methods.transfer: Sending halves of EPR pairs forces a prover to commit to a maximally mixed register it cannot bias. Pairing that with uncomputation and a SWAP test is a general way to test whether a classical sampler's image can be made exactly uniform.
